analysis.evidence: In וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ, “and these are the generations of Noah’s sons,” אֵלֶּה is the subject of a verbless clause. It points forward to the genealogy that follows.
analysis.morphology: וְ is the prefixed conjunction “and.” אֵלֶּה is a common-gender plural demonstrative pronoun.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 67081:1, 66817:2.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine plural construct, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: generations, the account of what came from someone

draft.change: Add Genesis 10:1 as evidence for the existing ben-son sense of בֵּן in the Haqor article ben.
draft.definition: A male child in relation to his father or mother.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:1 identifies בְּנֵי נֹחַ by name as Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 10:1 names Shem, Ham, and Japheth immediately after בְּנֵי נֹחַ, identifying the three men as Noah’s sons. The verse then says that sons were born to them, distinguishing the two generations.
analysis.morphology: Common masculine noun in the plural construct. The ending ־ֵי marks the plural construct, and the following name נֹחַ identifies the father.
analysis.sense: A male child in relation to his parent.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for נֹחַ linked to the root article nuach.
draft.definition: Noah, the son whom Lamech names in hope of relief from toil.
draft.evidence: Genesis 5:29 gives the name נֹחַ and explains it through the wordplay on יְנַחֲמֵנוּ, “he will comfort us.”

analysis.evidence: The phrase בְּנֵי נֹחַ introduces Noah as the father of the three sons named immediately afterward, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It follows the construct plural בְּנֵי in בְּנֵי נֹחַ.

draft.change: Add Genesis 10:21 to the existing personal-name article as evidence identifying Shem.
draft.definition: Shem, one of Noah’s sons, brother of Japheth and ancestor of Eber’s descendants.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:21 identifies Shem by his relationship to Japheth and to Eber’s descendants.

analysis.evidence: In Genesis 10:1, בְּנֵי נֹחַ introduces the list of Noah’s sons. שֵׁם is the first son named, followed by Ham and Japheth.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Shem, son of Noah and brother of Japheth

draft.change: The current personal-name article already cites Genesis 7:13 as defining evidence.
draft.definition: Ham is one of Noah’s three sons.
draft.evidence: Genesis 7:13 names Ham with Shem and Japheth and identifies all three as Noah’s sons.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 10:1 names חָם between Shem and Japheth in the list introduced by בְּנֵי נֹחַ, “the sons of Noah.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The phrase בְּנֵי נֹחַ introduces the list שֵׁם חָם וָיָפֶת, identifying Japheth as the third named son of Noah.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וָ means “and.” יָפֶת is the pausal form of the proper name יֶפֶת.

analysis.evidence: בָּנִים is the plural subject, לָהֶם identifies Noah’s sons as the parents, and אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל places the births after the flood. The clause means ‘and sons were born to them after the flood.’
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ־ precedes a Niphal wayyiqtol verb in the third-person masculine plural. The ending ־וּ marks plural agreement. There is no pronominal suffix.

draft.change: Link לָהֶם to word 0 of the existing article le and add Genesis 10:1 as an example of its le-dative sense.
draft.definition: לְ marks the person to whom something is given or for whom it happens. With a birth, it can identify the parent to whom a child is born.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:1 names Shem, Ham, and Japheth immediately before saying that sons were born לָהֶם, “to them.”

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּוָּלְדוּ לָהֶם בָּנִים, “sons were born to them,” בָּנִים is the subject of the passive verb. The suffix in לָהֶם refers back to Noah’s three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לְ takes the form לָ before the third-person masculine plural pronominal suffix הֶם.
analysis.sense: Dative marking the fathers to whom sons were born.

draft.change: Specify in the existing Genesis 10:1 evidence for ben-son that the absolute plural בָּנִים denotes the sons born to the three named men.
draft.definition: A son, a male child in relation to his parents.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:1 says that בָּנִים were born to Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The birth clause establishes the direct parent-child relationship.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּוָּלְדוּ לָהֶם בָּנִים, “sons were born to them,” בָּנִים is the subject of the plural verb וַיִּוָּלְדוּ. The pronoun in לָהֶם refers to Shem, Ham, and Japheth, identifying them as the fathers of the sons born after the flood.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew common noun, masculine plural absolute. The ending ־ִים marks the plural. The noun has no prefix or pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַחַר governs הַמַּבּוּל (‘the flood’). The phrase dates the birth of the sons to the time after the flood.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Refresh the reference to the current article, which already cites Genesis 10:1 under the flood sense.
draft.definition: An inundation in which rising waters cover the land.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:1 uses the flood as a point in time, dating the births of Noah’s grandsons after it.

analysis.evidence: The phrase אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל, “after the flood,” dates the births of sons to Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The definite article identifies the flood that Noah and his family survived.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed definite article הַ doubles the initial מ of מַבּוּל, a masculine singular common noun in the absolute state.
